newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - United Healthcare on costs.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - United Healthcare on costs.

text.p: U.S. medical cost inflation is holding steady at an annualized three to four percent, with some signs of easing in the key pharmacy cost segment, United Healthcare Corp said on Wednesday.

In an interview with Reuters after remarks to investors at a Piper Jaffray conference here, United chief operating officer Travers Wills said, "We haven't seen any dramatic step-up in costs anywhere."
On pharmacy costs, he said, "We'll see a much better trend this year...The pharmacy trend is nowhere near what it was last year."

United -- the largest U.S. for-profit health maintenance organization holding company -- was among the majority of U.S. HMOs blindsided in 1996 by an unexpected acceleration in medical cost inflation that outstripped annual premium increases and resulted in lower profit margins.

Much of the cost push last year was driven by price increases imposed on the healthcare system by major pharmaceutical manufacturers, but that pressure may be subsiding, contributing to more stable overall cost trends, Wills said.
"The trends are running a constant three or four and have been for a long time. We see no reason to be concerned about that," he said.
Other HMOs attending the Piper conference here confirmed the general trend.

United Healthcare "has been increasing commercial HMO prices by an average of five percent or more with medical costs trending three to four percent annually. We believe the combination of these factors will lead to more improved medical margins through the remainder of 1997," said Piper managed healthcare industry analyst John Penshorn.
With premium increases improving and costs appearing to level, United feels more confident that its projections this year will come closer to reality.

"When you've had a bad year like 1996, it's always a little uneasy to stand up and say we're just really on top of all this," Wills said. "But I believe we understand what went on (in 1996). I believe we have a handle on what led to the difficulties of 1996. I think we're on a track that's more solid in 1997."
The Minneapolis-based company's medical-loss ratio -- a key industry measure of profitability -- is in the 84 to 85 percent range, Wills said.
The company prefers the 81 to 84 percent range.
"We're looking to get down in the middle of that range by the end of the year," he said.
The ratio tells what percentage of premium revenues an HMO pays out to cover health plan members' medical costs, with the remainder largely covering certain internal costs and constituting profits.

"You get below 80 and we've always thought perhaps you weren't being responsible. I think as a company we've thought that. The range is always in the 81 to 84 range...That's a good pay-back to the customer," Wills said. "Right now we're sort of at the high end of that. We're 84, 85. I'd like to be down a couple points."
